title: Time-Series Decomposition with BASTION
text: Bayesian Adaptive Seasonality Trend decomposition Incorporating Outliers Noise (BASTION) Bayesian framework decomposing time series trend multiple seasonality. Existing decomposition methods, though widely used, exhibit several limitations: Difficulty adapting abrupt changes trend, Lack robustness outliers heteroskedasticity Absence uncertainty quantification, Inability accommodate multiple seasonal patterns, BASTION first Bayesian method effectively address challenges unified framework.

title: Time-Series Decomposition with BASTION
text: Let’s consider following simulated data : Figure 1: Simulated Data abrupt changes trend, outliers, Gaussian noise constant standard deviation 5. BASTION fitted along three existing methods comparison: TBATS (Alysha M. De Livera & Snyder, 2011) MSTL (Bandara et al., 2021) STR (Dokumentov & Hyndman, 2022). One defining characteristic simulated data see presence abrupt changes trend occur around t = 121, 158, 259. Figure 2: true trend component drawn black estimated trend component TBATS, MSTL, STR, BASTION drawn blue. Dotted lines represent BASTION’s 95 percent credible intervals STR’s 95 percent confidence intervals. Notice BASTION provides: Adaptive Trend Estimate: BASTION captures abrupt changes providing smooth estimates within segment. achieves lowest trend mean squared error (MSE) among four methods example. Robust Uncertainty Quantification: BASTION’s 95 percent credible intervals achieve 98.4 percent empirical coverage true trend. STR (Dokumentov & Hyndman, 2022) provides 95 percent confidence intervals 79 percent empirical coverage.
code: #devtools::install_github("Jasoncho0914/BASTION") library(BASTION) set.seed(40) BASTION_sim = fit_BASTION(y = y[,"y"],                       Ks = list(7,30),                       Outlier = TRUE,                       cl= 0.95,                       obsSV = "const",                       nsave = 2000,                       nburn = 5000,                       nchains = 2,                       nskip = 4,                       D_trend = 2,                       sparse = FALSE,                       verbose = FALSE,                       save_samples = TRUE) y_ts <- forecast::msts(y[,"y"], seasonal.periods=c(7,30)) TBATS = forecast::tbats(y_ts) TBATScomp = forecast::tbats.components(TBATS) STR = stR::AutoSTR(y_ts,robust = TRUE,confidence = 0.95) MSTL = forecast::mstl(y_ts) print(paste0(   "STR (Empirical Coverage): ",   sum(as.numeric(STR$output$predictors[[1]]$upper) > y[,"trend"] &        as.numeric(STR$output$predictors[[1]]$lower) < y[,"trend"])/length(y[,"trend"])*100,   "%")) #> [1] "STR (Empirical Coverage): 79%" print(paste0(   "BASTION (Empirical Coverage): ",   sum(as.numeric(BASTION_sim$intervals$upper$trend) > y[,"trend"] &        as.numeric(BASTION_sim$intervals$lower$trend) < y[,"trend"])/length(y[,"trend"])*100,   "%")) #> [1] "BASTION (Empirical Coverage): 98.4%"

Based raw data, see following: Seasonal Patterns: Electricity demand peaks summer months due air conditioning rises winter heating needs. Heteroskedasticity: Variability higher summer winter (periods peak demand) lower spring fall (stable usage). Long-Term Trends: significant long-term trend observed electricity demand. slight overall decline may indicate influence improved energy efficiency years.

title: Simulate data with known fixed seasonal periods — simulate_BASTION
text: scenario generates y sum known components independent zero-mean Gaussian noise. Time indexed observation number. "daily" generates 1095 observations fixed periods 7 365. t starting zero, trend 50 + 0.005*t. Weekly seasonality 3*cos(2*pi*(t+0.5)/7), yearly seasonality 8*sin(2*pi*(t+0.5)/365) + 2*cos(4*pi*(t+0.5)/365). Noise SD 1.5. "biweekly" generates 560 observations period 14. t starting zero, trend 100 + 0.01*t + 3*sin(2*pi*t/560), seasonality 6*sin(2*pi*t/14) + 2*cos(4*pi*t/14). Noise SD 1.5. "hourly" generates 2016 observations periods 24 168. t starting zero, trend 100 + 0.002*t. Using midpoint phase h within 24-observation cycle, daily seasonality 10*sin(2*pi*h) + 2*cos(4*pi*h). Weekly effects c(2, 3, 3, 2, 1, -5, -6), held 24 observations repeated every 168. Noise SD 2.

"daily" generates daily observations 2019 2021, including February 29, 2020. t starting zero, trend 50 + 0.005*t. Using midpoint calendar phases w within week within year, weekly seasonality 3*cos(2*pi*w), yearly seasonality 8*sin(2*pi*) + 2*cos(4*pi*). Noise SD 1.5. "biweekly" generates 560 daily observations starting January 6, 2020. t starting zero, trend 100 + 0.01*t + 3*sin(2*pi*t/560), seasonality 6*sin(2*pi*t/14) + 2*cos(4*pi*t/14). Noise SD 1.5. "hourly" generates 2016 hourly observations starting January 1, 2024 (12 full weeks). t starting zero, trend 100 + 0.002*t. Using midpoint phase h within day, daily seasonality 10*sin(2*pi*h) + 2*cos(4*pi*h). Monday--Sunday effects c(2, 3, 3, 2, 1, -5, -6), constant within day. Noise SD 2.
